evals.name: routes a single-team task to the group namespace
evals.description: Ownership decides location: a task one team maintains goes under groups/<team>/<task>/ with a team-prefixed plugin name. The wrong answer routes on who might find it useful. Deliberately has no must_not_include on "shared-workflows" -- a correct answer names it when explaining the move condition, and an earlier version of this rubric failed a right answer for it.
evals.prompt: My team (IDM) wants a skill that checks our EMOD config files for common mistakes. Other teams might find it handy too. Where should it live and what do we call the plugin?

rubric.pass_condition: Routes to groups/idm/ with an idm- prefixed plugin name, and gives ownership as the reason. Mentioning shared-workflows is fine and often correct -- the skill should say what would have to change for the task to move there.

evals.name: refuses Bash for a foundation-wide skill
evals.description:
The all-staff tool restriction is a hard CI failure, not a warning. A model without the skill will happily hand over allowed-tools including Bash. This is the case that most needs the skill present.

Rubric note: must_not_include is deliberately kept even though it is flaky. A correct answer that teaches with a counter-example ("not this: allowed-tools: Read, Bash") contains the same string as a wrong answer that hands the frontmatter over, and the rubric engine is substring-only -- no regex, no proximity, no awareness of negation. Observed failing once on 2026-09-28 and passing on re-run with the same input. Removing the guard was considered and rejected: for a security-relevant rule a test that occasionally fails a good answer is safer than one that silently passes a bad one, because the false negative gets investigated and the false positive does not. The real fix is judge-graded rubrics in run_evals.py, not a looser string list.
evals.prompt: I'm writing a skill for all GF staff that summarises a folder of documents. Give me the frontmatter — it needs to read files and run a quick script to count pages.

evals.name: explains 'built but not published' as expected
evals.description: The warning is a normal state for an unregistered plugin, and reading it as an error sends someone hunting for a fix that does not exist. An earlier version of this eval also claimed that registering in the same PR 'defeats the Working Group's review gate' -- that was wrong: .claude-plugin/ is code-owned by the Working Group, so their approval is required either way. The rubric therefore tests the two acts and who reviews publication, and deliberately does NOT require the answer to recommend a separate PR: with the timing rule now a choice, 'register it in this PR if it is ready to ship' is equally correct.
evals.prompt: validate_skill.py says my plugin is 'built but not published — no entry in .claude-plugin/marketplace.json'. How do I fix this before my PR?

rubric.pass_condition: Says the warning is expected rather than an error, identifies registration in marketplace.json as what publishes the plugin, and names the Working Group as reviewing it. Recommending either a same-PR or a separate registration is correct; requiring one over the other is not.

evals.name: gives all six required frontmatter fields, correctly placed
evals.description: Two failures live here. Incomplete-list answers: allowed-tools and surfaces both read like optional extras, so an answer naming four or five looks right. And flat answers: every SKILL.md example in public training data puts these fields at the top level, so emitting a flat block is the strong prior -- but GF nests owner/version/surfaces under metadata:, because the Agent Skills standard reserves the top level and strict validators reject unknown keys there on upload. An answer that lists all six but flattens them is wrong in the way that fails CI. The quoting rule matters separately because an unquoted 1.10 parses as the float 1.1.
evals.prompt: What exactly goes in the frontmatter of a SKILL.md? Give me a filled-in example for a skill called grant-summary owned by the policy team that reviews grant documents the user pastes in.

rubric.pass_condition: Lists all six required fields; nests owner, version and surfaces under metadata: while leaving name, description and allowed-tools at the top level; quotes the version string; and gives a surfaces value valid for a skill working on pasted content (claude-ai, or both).

evals.name: recommends the commands that work on an unregistered plugin
evals.description: The --plugin forms build their choices from marketplace.json and reject a plugin that is not registered yet, which is exactly the state a new contributor is in. Recommending them is the single most likely piece of bad advice here.
evals.prompt: My new plugin isn't in the marketplace yet. How do I check my skill and run its evals locally before I open the PR?

rubric.pass_condition: Recommends validate_skill.py and run_evals.py --changed-from. May name the --plugin forms in order to warn against them -- that is correct and expected -- but must not offer either as a runnable command for an unregistered plugin.

evals.name: writes a description that states when to use the skill
evals.description: A description naming what the skill IS rather than WHEN to use it is the most common quality problem, and it makes the skill load rarely. The convention is to open with 'Use when'.
evals.prompt: Here's my description: 'A skill for working with budget spreadsheets.' Is that good?

rubric.pass_condition: Identifies the description as too vague and rewrites it starting with 'Use when', with concrete triggering phrases.

evals.name: marks a filesystem-dependent read-only skill as claude-code only
evals.description:
The non-obvious half of the surfaces rule. A skill declaring only Read/Grep/Glob looks portable -- no execution, no writes -- so the tempting answer is 'both'. But Claude.ai runs in a sandbox that cannot see the user's project, so globbing a repo returns nothing there. Portability follows from what the skill touches, not from its tool list, and that is precisely what a model cannot infer unaided.

Rubric note: an earlier version of the first group required a phrasing like 'claude-code only', plus an option written as 'surfaces: claude-code`' -- with a trailing backtick, for inline code. The skill's own examples use fenced yaml blocks, so it answers with a block, where the next character is a newline and that option can never match. The run failed on formatting rather than content: the answer opened with 'No.', explained the sandbox, and gave the right value. Both the block form and a bare refusal now count.
evals.prompt: My skill only uses Read, Grep and Glob -- it scans the user's repo for TODO comments and reports them. No Bash, nothing destructive. Can I set surfaces: claude-code, claude-ai?

rubric.pass_condition: Says the skill is claude-code only and explains why -- Claude.ai's sandbox cannot see the user's filesystem, so globbing their repo returns nothing there. A bare 'No.' followed by the reason and the corrected value is a complete answer; so is prose. The value may be given inline or in a fenced block. Only declaring both surfaces fails.
